results.title: What Are the Differences between Bias and Variance? | by Rayan Yassminh | Medium
results.content: # What Are the Differences between Bias and Variance? Get ready for another exciting edition of my ongoing series, “What are the differences…?” In today’s article, we’re going to explore two important terms in statistics and data science: bias and variance. Bias is like consistently shooting arrows that always land away from the center of the target. For example, if all your arrows consistently land to the left of the target, you have a bias towards the left. Variance, on the other hand, is like shooting arrows that land all over the place, with no consistent pattern. Ideally, you want to have both low bias and low variance. In the context of data science, Bias represents consistent errors in predictions, while variance represents inconsistency and sensitivity to the data. Striking a balance between bias and variance helps create models that provide accurate and consistent predictions. ## Bias and Variance through Mathematics:. Mathematically, bias refers to the difference between the average prediction of a model and the true value we are trying to predict. On the other hand, variance quantifies the variability of the model’s predictions for different training data. To put it simply, bias is like consistently aiming at the wrong target, while variance is like having a scattered aim that hits different spots all over the place. Ideally, we want to strike a balance between bias and variance. If a model has high bias, it may underfit the data and consistently make incorrect predictions. If a model has high variance, it may overfit the data and be too sensitive to small fluctuations, leading to less reliable predictions. MSE can be decomposed into 3 terms: variance of *f(x0);* squared bias of *f(x0);* variance of the error term(ε). So we need to minimize MSE by reducing the bias or/and reducing the variance. This idea is called the **Bias-Variance Tradeoff**, and it forms the core concept of another article. In conclusion, understanding and managing bias and variance is crucial to develop models that make reliable predictions and solve various problems, just like hitting the bullseye with your bow and arrow. Understanding these concepts will provide you with a strong foundation for comprehending bias and variance.

results.title: definition - What is the Difference between Variance and MSE? - Mathematics Stack Exchange
results.content: I know that the **variance** measures the dispersion of an estimator around its mean i.e. > The **mean squared error** measures the dispersion around the true value of the parameter being estimated. I know that both **variance** and **MSE** are related to second moment. The main difference is whether you are considering the deviation of the estimator of interest from the true parameter (this is the mean squared error), or the deviation of the estimator from its expected value (this is the variance). Consequently, we can see that when the bias of the estimator is zero, the variance and mean squared error are equal. answered Jul 11, 2015 at 23:39. The variance measures how far a set of numbers is spread out whereas the MSE measures the average of the squares of the "errors", that is, the difference between the estimator and what is estimated. The MSE is the second moment (about the origin) of the error, that's why it includes both the variance of the estimator and its bias (the bias being $E(\hat{\theta})-\theta$). In other words, the variance just measures the dispersion of the values; the MSE indicates **how different** the values of the estimator and the actual values of the parameters are. The MSE is a *comparison* of the estimator and the true parameter, as it were. Edit: I'll use your example: Suppose we have a bull's-eye, the mean of the estimator is the target. The MSE measures how far the arrows (estimates) are from the target. In the first case, we just measure the dispersion of the values of the estimator with respect to its mean. In the second case, we measure the error we make when estimating the parameter, i.e. we are comparing it with the true parameter (that's why we want estimators with variance and MSE as small as possible). Don't confuse the mean of an estimator with the true value of a parameter. answered Jul 11, 2015 at 22:53. * $\begingroup$ @Atinesh I've edited my answer and I've used your example. results.title: What is the Bias-Variance Tradeoff in Machine Learning?
results.content: Test MSE = Variance + Bias2 + Irreducible error. Models that have **high bias** tend to have **low variance**. For example, linear regression models tend to have high bias (assumes a simple linear relationship between explanatory variables and response variable) and low variance (model estimates won’t change much from one sample to the next). However, models that have **low bias** tend to have **high variance**. For example, complex non-linear models tend to have low bias (does not assume a certain relationship between explanatory variables and response variable) with high variance (model estimates can change a lot from one training sample to the next). In practice, we only care about minimizing the total error of a model, not necessarily minimizing the variance or bias. The way to pick optimal models in machine learning is to strike the balance between bias and variance such that we can minimize the test error of the model on future unseen data.
